The act of agitating, or the state of being agitated; the state of being disrupted with violence, or with irregular action; commotion.

examples.text: During a storm the sea is in agitation.

glosses: A disturbance of personal tranquillity; disturbance of someone's peace of mind.

examples.text: She causes great agitation within me.

glosses: Excitement of public feeling by discussion, appeals, etc.

examples.text: the antislavery agitation
labor agitation
After this conflict pro-independence agitation temporarily died down.
[…] religious agitations […]

glosses: Examination or consideration of a subject in controversy, or of a plan proposed for adoption; earnest discussion; debate.

examples.text: […] a logical agitation of the matter […]
[…] the project now in agitation […]

glosses: Putting into motion by shaking or stirring, often to achieve mixing.
The state of being discomposed.

examples.text: And now it was that I began to keep a journal of every day's employment; for, indeed, at first I was in too much hurry, and not only hurry as to labour, but in too much discomposure of mind; and my journal would have been full of many dull things[.]
"The real reason is that some small element of danger is involved in our experiment, though it is not sufficient to justify the discomposure which I see upon many of your faces."

glosses: Discordance; disagreement of parts.

examples.text: But this is wrought by emission , or suppression , or suffocation , of the native spirits ; and also by the disordination and discomposure of the tangible parts , and other passages of nature , and not by a conflict of heats

glosses: The state of being excited (emotionally aroused).

examples.text: to get caught up in the excitement
By late accounts from Rotterdam, that city seems to be in a high state of philosophical excitement.

In 1825, the first public railway carried passengers across the English countryside, setting in motion not just an engineering revolution, but an industrial one too. Imagine the awe and excitement of those first passengers as they boarded the train, unaware that they were witnessing the dawn of a new era.

glosses: Something that excites.
The state or fact of being turbulent or agitated; tempestuousness, disturbance.

examples.text: Turbulence was everywhere, within every blade of grass, every drop of dew on a leaf, every cloud in the sky, and every star beyond. The turbulence was purposeless, but in huge quantities of purposeless turbulence, purpose took shape.

glosses: Disturbance in a gas or fluid, characterized by evidence of internal motion or unrest.
Specifically, a state of agitation or disturbance in the air which is disruptive to an aircraft.
An instance or type of such state or disturbance.

examples.text: In a brief and abashed Tory conference speech, Kwarteng admitted it had been a “tough day” – hours after rowing back on the tax cut for high earners. He said his economic plan had caused “a little turbulence”.

glosses: Agitation; the state of being perturbed

examples.text: Reſtore your ſelues, vnto your temper, Fathers; / And, vvithout perturbation, heare me ſpeake: […]
But her mind had never been in such perturbation; and it needed a very strong effort to appear attentive and cheerful till the usual hour of separating allowed her the relief of quiet reflection.

glosses: A small change in a physical system, or more broadly any definable system (such as a biological or economic system)

examples.text: Natures that haue much Heat, and great and violent deſires and Perturbations, are not ripe for Action, till they haue paſſed the Meridian of their yeares: As it was with Iulius Cæſar, and Septimius Seuerus.

glosses: Variation in an orbit due to the influence of external bodies
To disturb the relative position of the particles (of a liquid or similar) by passing an object through it.

examples.text: She stirred the pudding with a spoon.
He stirred his coffee so the sugar wouldn't stay at the bottom.
My minde is troubled, like a Fountaine stir'd, / And I my selfe see not the bottome of it.

glosses: To disturb the content of (a container) by passing an object through it.

examples.text: Would you please stir this pot so that the chocolate doesn't burn?

glosses: To emotionally affect; to touch, to move.

examples.text:
And what delights can equal those
⁠That stir the spirit’s inner deeps,
⁠When one that loves but knows not, reaps
A truth from one that loves and knows?

glosses: To incite to action.

examples.text: An Ate, stirring him to bloud and strife […]
The Soldiers love her Brother’s Memory; / And for her sake some Mutiny will stir.

glosses: To bring into debate; to agitate.

examples.text: Preserue the rights of thy place, but stirre not questions of Iurisdiction : and rather assume thy right in silence, and de facto, then voice it with claimes, and challenges.

glosses: To disturb, to disrupt.

examples.text:

glosses: To change the place of in any manner; to move.

examples.text: […] notwithstanding the swelling of my Foot, so that I had never yet in five days been able to stir it, but as it was lifted.

glosses: To begin to move, especially gently, from a still or unmoving position.

examples.text: And especially if they happen to have any superior character or possessions in this world, they fancy they have a right to talk freely upon everything that stirs or appears[…]

glosses: Of a feeling or emotion: to rise, begin to be felt.

examples.text: That night he was almost too happy to sleep, and so much love stirred in his little sawdust heart that it almost burst.

glosses: To be in motion; to be active or bustling; to exert or busy oneself.

examples.text: All are not fit with them to stir and toil.

glosses: To rise from sleep or unconsciousness.
